newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ govt MP slammed for seeking cash for interview.
newsitem.headline: NZ govt MP slammed for seeking cash for interview.

text.p: New Zealand government MP Tukoroirangi Morgan admitted on Thursday that he had sought payment for a television interview in a move that has enraged politicians and generated widespread media attention.
The Maori MP is a member of New Zealand First, the junior partner in New Zealand's centre-right coalition government that has a fragile one-seat majority in the 120-member parliament.

He had at first denied claims made by two television stations on Wednesday evening that a lawyer claiming to represent Morgan, who is in the middle of two libel actions, had offered to sell them his story for more than NZ$20,000 ($14,000).

But on Thursday, Morgan issued a statement admitting he had instructed that the contacts be made, embarassing his party leader and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters, who on Wednesday night backed up his MP's initial denial.
In a strongly-worded media statement, Peters said Morgan's approaches to the media were totally wrong and had occurred without his knowledge or that of his office.
"Had I been approached, I would have told Mr Morgan categorically that such approaches are plainly wrong."
Peters said any repetition of a mistake of this nature "will result in severe consequences".
Morgan said on Thursday that he needed to cover the expenses of two defamation cases he was involved in that his barrister, Peter Williams, told radio news could come to $100,000.
One is a libel action he is pursuing against opposition Labour Party MP Trevor Mallard. He is also defending himself against a defamation suit from a Maori tribal trust.
Prime Minister Jim Bolger, who leads the conservative National Party in the two-party coalition, rebuked Morgan's attitude and said he sympathised with Peters.
Though he did not issue a formal comment, a spokesman for his office told Reuters that Bolger found the MP's behaviour "unacceptable and inappropriate".

Asked how the premier took issue with what Morgan had done, spokesman Richard Griffin said Bolger believed "that it is not the business of politicans and parliamentarians to be asking for money for interviews.
"They are public persona and as such, (media access) is part of the burden of office," he added.
On Wednesday in Wellington, Morgan denied the claim that an Auckland-based lawyer who contacted the press, Chris Reid, was acting on his instructions.
On Wednesday evening, TV3 played a taped conversation with Reid in which he said Morgan was going to have difficulties with finances so was looking for an offer.
"If you are prepared to pay for an interview, he'd give it to you exclusively," Reid told a TV3 news reporter.

In his about-turn statement issued on Thursday, Morgan admitted, "Through my barrister Peter Williams QC I gave instructions that Chris Reid be engaged to enter into negotiations of a confidental nature with the news media...".

Morgan and Williams sought to explain the MP's change of heart over the issue by saying there were telephone problems between Morgan and Reid during Wednesday afternoon when they were in different cities.

Morgan's political career has been marred by his involvement prior to his entering parliament with publicly funded pilot Maori language broadcaster Aotearoa Television Network (ATN), which is being investigated the Serious Fraud Office.
He has been heavily criticised in recent months for refusing media interviews on the ATN affair and ducking questions in parliament, saying the matter was sub judice.
